Tinted yellow everywhere in the app. Reply to customer Service projects only. A comment the customer sees on the portal and receives by email. It cannot be recalled. Second comment One request carrying both — a reply and the internal note behind it, written separately and posted together. The send guard The confirmation that appears before a risky send, counting what is about to go out. Ready / Status only A composer with something to post / a composer that will only move status. An untouched composer carries no badge and is skipped. Batch The issues you picked, taken together. One send posts one batch.

Everything in the app is reachable without a mouse, and the places where that is easy to get wrong were rebuilt rather than patched. Nothing is hover-only. The × on a list row, the Only shortcut on a status, the controls on a composer header — all of them are always rendered, because a control that appears on hover cannot be reached by Tab . The list down the left opens on focus , not only on hover, so tabbing into the rail expands it. Menus behave like menus. Opening the ••• menu or the status picker puts focus on the first item; ↑ and ↓ wrap around; Home and End jump to the ends; Esc closes and puts focus back on the button you opened it from, so you never lose your place. The confirmation dialog traps focus and starts on Cancel — deliberately, because a button fires on Enter being pressed down, so starting on the send button could post the batch with the same keypress that opened the dialog. Esc cancels, and focus returns to where it was. Progress is announced. The composer disappears the moment a send starts, so the line reporting progress is a live region — a screen-reader user hears the send run and hears its outcome, rather than silence. Selected issues are announced as checkboxes , with their state. At the 25 ceiling the remaining rows stay reachable and explain why they cannot be picked, instead of being switched off and going silent. Every control says what it will do to which issue — not “Remove” but “Remove PAY-412 from this batch”, not “Only” but “Show only In Review”. Keyboard focus is always visible , and the image viewer is a proper dialog with Esc and arrow keys.

There is no theme setting, because the app has no theme of its own. It renders in whichever colour scheme Jira hands it — including the editor, the status lozenges and the readiness badges, which are tinted per scheme rather than inverted. Every screen in this guide looks like this in dark: Dark mode follows Jira’s own colour scheme — nothing is switched in the app.

Everything below is stored in your own browser, on your own machine. None of it is sent anywhere, and none of it is visible to anyone else — clearing your browser data clears all of it. Your comments, as you type them — every composer’s draft is saved continuously, so a refresh, an accidental tab close or a Jira navigation does not cost you the batch you have written. Reopening the app restores the drafts and re-selects the issues they belong to, so you land back where you were rather than on an empty Select step. The layout — whether the issue list on the left is pinned open or collapsed to a rail, whether the details panel is open, and the width you dragged each of them to. Recently seen issues — a small cache of issue summaries so a batch restored from a draft can show its titles immediately rather than blank rows while Jira answers. Clear all comments & status changes clears the saved drafts too, so it is the deliberate way to start over rather than something you have to hunt for.

Everything you write is posted as native Jira formatting, so a comment sent from here is indistinguishable from one typed into Jira itself — same headings, same tables, same code blocks, same file cards. The toolbar and the keyboard shortcuts deliberately mirror Jira's own editor, so there is nothing new to learn. Shortcuts below are written in Mac notation. On Windows and Linux read ⌘ as Ctrl , ⇧ as Shift and ⌥ as Alt . The app detects your machine and shows the right one in every tooltip.

The dropdown at the far left of the toolbar sets the current block. It shows what you are currently in, so you can always tell whether the cursor is inside a heading. Block Shortcut Normal text ⌘⌥0 Heading 1 through Heading 6 ⌘⌥1 … ⌘⌥6

Control Shortcut Bold ⌘B Italic ⌘I Underline ⌘U Strikethrough ⌘⇧S Subscript ⌘, Superscript ⌘. Inline code ⌘⇧M Text colour — 28 Atlassian palette colours, plus Remove colour Toolbar A button Undo / Redo ⌘Z / ⌘Y
Block Shortcut Bullet list ⌘⇧8 Numbered list ⌘⇧7 Task list — checkboxes your team can tick off on the issue, and they nest ⌘⇧6 Quote ⌘⇧B Divider Type /divider

The table button opens a size grid — drag across it to choose how many rows and columns you want. Once the cursor is inside a table, a second row of controls appears with everything you need to reshape it: Header row and Header col — toggle either independently, so a table can have a header row, a header column, both, or neither. Add columns before or after the current one, and add rows above or below. Delete table to remove the whole thing in one click.

A code block keeps your indentation and monospacing intact, and carries a language selector with 42 languages — Bash, C, C++, C#, CSS, Dart, Go, GraphQL, Groovy, Haskell, HTML, Java, JavaScript, JSON, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, Rust, SQL, TypeScript, YAML and more, plus (None) for plain text. The language travels with the comment, so Jira highlights it correctly on every issue you post to.

Type / anywhere in the editor to open a command palette, exactly like Jira's. Keep typing to filter the list, move with the arrow keys, and press Enter to insert. Twelve commands are available, so you never have to reach for the toolbar mid-sentence: Command What it inserts /image · Image, video, or file Attach a file to this comment /heading 1 Large section heading /heading 2 Medium section heading /heading 3 Small section heading /bullet list Unordered list /numbered list Ordered list /task list Action items with checkboxes /quote Blockquote /divider Horizontal rule /code block Code snippet with language selector /table Opens the size picker /emoji Opens the emoji browser It matches on synonyms. The attachment command is called “Image, video, or file”, but /screenshot , /upload , /photo , /media , /attach and /video all find it. The palette opens mid-sentence , not just at line start.

@mentions — type @ ; a bare @ lists teammates. Only people are suggested — apps and service-project customers are filtered out. Mentioned people are notified on every issue the comment lands on, which is why a mention always asks you to confirm first. Smart links — paste a Jira or Confluence URL and it becomes a live card showing title, status, priority and assignee, fetched fresh. Click it for a Display as menu: URL , Inline , Card or Embed . Emoji — browse from the toolbar or type /emoji .

Attach files three ways: drag them into the editor, paste a screenshot straight from the clipboard, or use the toolbar button. Dropping a file places it where your pointer is, not where the cursor happened to be. Up to 150 MB per file , with no limit on how many files one comment can carry. If your Jira site sets a lower attachment limit, that one wins — the app reads the site's real limit and checks against it the moment you attach, so an oversized file is refused immediately rather than after you have written the comment. Uploading starts on attach, not on Send. The file moves while you are still typing, so the send itself is usually near-instant — the attachment shows Uploading… while it goes, or Will upload when you send if it could not start early. Nothing is visible on any issue until you actually send, and anything you attach and then delete is discarded. Images and video preview inline , align left, centre or right, and resize by dragging the edge — the same handles Jira gives you. PDFs and other documents post as file cards. Large files upload through an async queue in the background , so a long video posting to 25 issues does not block the send while it uploads. A file is refused the moment you attach it, not at send , and the message names which limit bound — your site's, or the app's 150 MB. The oversized file is dropped; the rest of the batch still attaches. Select an attachment and a toolbar appears on it — align, card or inline, reset, download, full size, duplicate, remove. Images and video resize by dragging their edge ; the width is stored as a percentage, so it scales in whatever width the reader's Jira gives the comment. Duplicating an attachment costs nothing. The copy points at the same upload, so putting one screenshot in two places in a comment does not upload it twice. Previews are generated on your own machine — nothing is sent anywhere to make them. Video gets a poster frame and a player with ±10 seconds, speed and fullscreen; a PDF shows page one; logs, CSVs and code show their first twelve lines; anything else gets a typed file card. Removing an attachment releases it. The staged copy is deleted straight away rather than sitting in storage until it expires. And a draft reopened after a reload keeps the attachment’s place but not its bytes — it reads re-attach — file not kept after reload , and correctly does not count as something to send. A whole send is capped at 2 GB across the batch — separate from the 150 MB per file, so every file can be inside its own limit and the send still be refused. Four 120 MB files to 5 issues is 2400 MB and will not send. See Limits .

t: Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management
h: Choose who reads it — internal note or customer reply
x: On a Jira Service Management or Customer Service Management request, a comment is one of two different things. An Internal note is seen by agents only. A Reply to customer reaches the customer and emails them. They are never the same sentence, and on a batch of twenty-five that difference is the whole job. Every request starts on Reply to customer . That is the default because an agent bulk-commenting on a service project is usually answering customers, and an internal note is the exception. Switch a request to Internal and it stays there — the default is only ever applied to a request you have not decided on yet, so it cannot come back and undo your choice. So every service-project composer carries the choice in its header. It is per request, not per send — one run can answer three customers and leave two notes for the team. Issues from Jira and Jira Product Discovery have no such distinction and show no control; their comments are simply comments. Yellow means internal, everywhere — the toggle, the tint on a comment box, the badges in comment history and the badges on the results screen. The accent colour is anything the customer receives. It is Jira’s own convention in the service project issue view. A reply to a customer cannot be taken back. The email is gone the moment it posts. This is why there is no undo, and why the confirmation before a send names exactly how many customers that send will reach — that number is the last thing you see before it goes.

t: Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management
h: Put both on one request — a reply and a note
x: Answering a customer usually leaves something to record that the customer should not read: what actually caused it, what you tried, what to watch next time. One request can carry both. Add a second comment sits at the foot of a service-project composer, naming the audience it will add — internal note on a composer set to reply to the customer, reply to customer on one set to internal. Press it and a second box opens beneath the first. Write them separately; they post together as one issue’s work. The composer is stacked the way Jira will show it. Jira lists newest first, so the comment that posts last ends up on top. The upper box reads posted last · shows on top , the lower one posted first . To swap them, use Move up on the lower box. Both still post — it only changes which one ends up on top. The second box is always the opposite audience to the first, so a pair can never drift into two comments that both go to the customer. Close it with the × on its header and the composer goes back to a single comment. On a composer carrying both, the Internal / Reply to customer toggle swaps the two comments, text and all — the same action as Move up , from the header. Your sentences travel with their audience; the toggle only decides which ends up on top. A composer written only in its second box still sends — the note posts as that issue’s one comment, carrying its own audience. This is why twenty-five issues can produce fifty comments. The cap the app enforces is on issues, not comments — see Limits .

t: Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management
x: Two of the batch controls on the Comment step exist only for service projects, because only a request can carry a second, internal comment. Both name the number they will actually affect — on a mixed batch that is the service-project requests in it, not everything you picked.

t: Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management
h: Working across the whole batch › Opening and removing internal notes
x: Add internal note to n requests — opens a second, internal box on every request that can have one and does not already, ready to type into. It writes nothing for you ; the boxes arrive empty so you can say something different on each. Delete all internal notes — the reverse. It takes the boxes away along with whatever is in them. It only asks twice when something is written in them — open a box on every request, change your mind, and one press closes them all, because there is nothing to lose. Clearing is not the same as deleting. Clear all comments & status changes empties your internal notes but leaves the boxes open, because it names comments and status changes and a box is neither. If you want the boxes gone, Delete all internal notes is the one.

t: Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management
h: Working across the whole batch › Copying with two audiences
x: A request can hold two comments and they are not interchangeable, so the ••• menu carries one entry per audience : Copy this comment to n issues (reply to customer only) — the label says so explicitly, so it can never drop your customer-facing wording into somebody’s internal note. Copy this comment to n internal notes — the same for the other half. Neither action opens a box, and neither changes any composer’s audience. A reply copies onto replies and a note onto notes, so copying can never turn an internal note into a customer email. That is also why the two counts usually differ from each other, and from the size of the batch. The rest of the Comment step — the editor, the details panel, status changes — works the same on a request as anywhere else: see Step 2 — Comment .

Pick up to 25 issues. Find the issues you want and tick up to 25 of them. Everything you can see in Jira is listed by default; the controls along the top narrow it down, and the tray along the bottom holds everything you have picked — even across several different searches — and counts it against the 25. More than 25? Send in batches. Filter down to the first 25 — Select all visible with a project or status filter takes a whole group in two clicks — send them, then press Done and pick the next 25. Anything you wrote on issues you have not sent yet is kept, so you can build the next batch straight away.

h: Search, filter and sort the issue list
x: The controls along the top of the Select step, left to right. Every one is applied inside the Jira query rather than to the rows already on screen, so they reorder the whole result set. Search — by keyword or issue key, in Basic or JQL mode. Filtering and sorting happen inside the query, so they reorder the whole result set rather than the rows on screen. A full issue key ignores every filter. Type MYQ-3 and you get it, even if it is Done or in a filtered-out project. A partial key is a project prefix and does respect filters, as does keyword search — which matches the summary , not the description. In JQL mode the query is authoritative, so the project, status, assignee and sort controls disappear. Enter runs it; ⇧Enter is a new line. Project — defaults to All projects , and appears once you have seen more than one. The list only ever grows , so narrowing to one never strands you. It carries its own Search projects field, matching name or key. Every row carries a small mark before its summary, so a mixed list stays readable at a glance: Lightning bolt — Jira Service Management Person — Customer Service Management Lightbulb — Jira Product Discovery — No mark — Jira, the ordinary case The mark matters because it tells you which issues will offer a Reply to customer choice on the next step. Only the first two ever do. Status — tick what you want to see. The names come from each project’s workflow , not the rows loaded, so you get your own wording and can filter to a status with nothing on screen yet. Narrowing the project narrows this list too. Done is hidden by default. Three shortcuts: Select all / Deselect all — one toggle at the top of the list, which flips depending on where you are Only — every status carries one, with a count beside it. It jumps straight to that single status instead of making you untick the other nine Reset to open issues — back to the default in one press The header then reads how many you have hidden, so a filtered list never looks like an empty one — and if you switch every status off, it says No statuses selected, so no issues can match. Pick at least one. rather than showing you a blank list with no explanation. Statuses with nothing in them collapse behind a Show n empty statuses line. Assigned to me — off by default, so you see everyone’s issues. One click narrows the list to only the issues assigned to you; click again to see everyone’s. Sort — three fields, each taking its natural direction first: Updated — most recently changed first Issue key — by key, so a project’s issues run in order Summary — alphabetical, A–Z The arrow beside the field flips between ascending and descending. Select all visible — ticks every issue currently on screen, up to the 25 ceiling. Once everything visible is picked it flips to Deselect all and clears them, so it is its own undo. Pair it with the project filter and you can take a whole project in two clicks.

h: The selection tray, and the 25 ceiling
x: The tray along the bottom lists every issue you have picked, no matter which search you found it in — so a selection built from three different queries is still visible in one place, with the counter reading n / 25 selected . Press the × on any chip to drop that issue without going back to hunt for it. At 25 — the ceiling is on issues, not comments — the unpicked rows dim and explain themselves with Selection is limited to 25 . Select all visible flips to Deselect all .

h: What happens when you open the app
x: When you open the app the previous list paints immediately from your browser while the fresh search runs behind it. Every issue carried over from a draft is checked against Jira at the same time; anything deleted or out of reach is dropped with a notice naming it — PAY-412 is no longer available — removed.

Write a different comment on each issue. Write a separate comment on every issue you picked. Each one is its own composer with its own editor, attachments and status change, and you land on the list already able to type. The issues run down the left so you can jump between them, the composers sit in the middle, and a panel on the right shows the full detail of whichever composer you are on.

h: How the screen is laid out
x: Three regions, left to right. Everything on this step lives in one of them. Issue navigation — every issue in the batch, listed down the left. Click one to jump to it. The comment composer — one per issue, stacked in the middle. Each carries its own comment editor, its own attachments and its own status change, which is what makes twenty-five different comments possible in one pass. The details panel — on the right, and read-only. It shows the full detail of whichever composer you are writing in: description, fields, attachments and the issue’s own comment history. Nothing is posted from this step. Everything you write is held until you send it on Step 3, and drafts survive if you leave and come back.

Twenty-five issues on one page is a lot to scroll through. The strip down the left lists every issue in the batch, so you can jump straight to the one you want instead of hunting for it. Click a row and that issue scrolls into view. Nothing else closes — every composer stays open and editable, so you can watch a copied comment land on the ones further down. Each row shows the issue key, its summary, the status change if you queued one, and a dot that fills in once that issue has something to send. You can leave the strip narrow, peek at it, or pin it open: Narrow — just the dots. Takes almost no width, and you can still click a row. Peek — hover over it, or tab to it, and the full list slides out on top. It sits over the composers rather than pushing them aside, so whatever you are typing in stays where it is. Pinned — the list stays open in its own column and the composers shift across to make room. The app remembers this between visits. Press the × on any row to drop that issue from the batch.

h: What is on a comment composer
x: One issue, one box. Each composer holds everything you can set for that issue — its comment, its attachments, its status change, and on a service project its audience. Reading the header from left to right: Issue key and Details › — one control. The key or the title opens the details panel; neither opens Jira. To reach the issue, use the key chip inside the panel — it carries an ↗ . The Details › label drops away once the panel is open. Internal / Reply to customer — service projects only. These appear on Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management issues and nowhere else. ••• — that composer’s actions: copy its comment across the batch, copy its internal note across the batch, or clear it. Each entry names the real number it will affect. See Copy one comment across the batch . × — drops that issue. One click, no confirmation, because it does not throw away what you wrote : pick the issue again at Step 1 and its comment, note, status change and audience all come back. The same × is on every row of the list. Beneath the header, at a glance, is the issue’s summary , who it is assigned to — or Unassigned — when it was last commented on , and a Ready badge once the composer has something to send. Enough to know what you are writing about without opening anything. Status sits under the comment box, not in the header. On a request carrying two comments it sits below both, so it is always the last thing on the composer.

Every composer has a full editor that posts native Jira formatting — headings, tables, code blocks, mentions, emoji and attachments up to 150 MB per file — with the same toolbar and shortcuts as Jira’s own. The comment editor: every format and shortcut →

You often need to read an issue before you can write about it. Press Details › beside the key, or the issue title, and the panel opens on the right showing that issue as Jira holds it. It is read-only, and separate from what you are typing. It follows you. Scroll to the next issue, or jump to one from the left, and the panel is already describing it. One panel, always about the composer in front of you.

h: The details panel › What it shows
x: You cannot change what appears here or what order it comes in — there is nothing to configure. What you can do is collapse any section you are not using, and that choice sticks as you scroll down the batch. Description — the issue’s description, rendered as Jira renders it. Details — the field grid, below. Attachments — only appears when the issue actually has attachments. Collapsing it is how you stop previews loading for every issue you scroll past. All comments — the issue’s comment history.

h: The details panel › The field grid
x: Seven fields are always there, showing None when the issue has nothing in them: Type · Assignee · Reporter · Parent · Priority · Due date · Labels After those come every other field the issue has a value for — Sprint, Story points, Components, Team, Start date and any custom field your site adds — each under the name Jira itself shows for it, in alphabetical order. Created and Updated sit at the foot. Empty fields are left out, so the grid stays as short as the issue is. A custom field added to your Jira next week appears here on its own; nothing needs setting up in the app. Fields Jira exposes without a readable name are skipped rather than shown as customfield_10042 . Above the grid, subtasks and linked work items are listed by relationship when the issue has them, and each opens in Jira.

h: The details panel › The comment history
x: The list shows the 25 most recent comments , in full. The section header carries a count — 7 on an issue with seven, and 25+ once there are more than twenty-five. On a capped issue a note sits under the list — “Showing the 25 most recent. Open in Jira for the full history.” — so you always know whether you are looking at everything. Images, video and files in that history play or preview right there: video plays inline with a thumbnail before you click, and images open in a full-size viewer you can arrow through. You never have to leave for Jira to find out what a past comment attached. On a service project, each past comment says who saw it. A Customer badge in the accent colour, or Internal in yellow — so before writing a reply you can see what the customer has already been told, and what was only ever said to the team. Those badges appear only on service-project issues, because nowhere else does the distinction exist.

h: The details panel › Opening in Jira, and resizing
x: The key chip in the panel header carries an ↗ and opens the issue in a new tab, leaving what you have written untouched. Subtasks, linked work items and individual comments open the same way. Both side panels are resizable, and the width is remembered between sessions. On a narrow window they give way rather than squeezing you: the editor keeps a 560-pixel floor, and a pinned issue list drops back to its narrow strip if the panel would push the editor below that. Attachments on the comment you are writing work the same way, right there in the composer, up to 150 MB per file — see The comment editor .

Everywhere else in Jira a comment is just a comment. On Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management it also decides whether a customer is emailed, so three things change — and only on those requests: Every request carries an audience — Internal or Reply to customer , set in its header, per request. A request can carry both at once — a customer reply and an internal note, written separately and posted together. Two extra batch controls appear, for opening and removing internal notes across every request in one go. Nothing on this page changes for an ordinary issue: it takes one comment, with no audience to choose. The full detail — including which comment posts first and why it matters — is on Jira Service Management and Customer Service Management .

A status dropdown sits under each comment editor. Leave it alone and nothing happens to that issue’s status — it is optional, and set per issue. Open it and you get that issue’s own workflow transitions, so only moves Jira would accept. Pick one and the button shows where the issue is heading; × clears it. Where a transition’s name differs from where it lands, the menu shows both — Respond to customer → Waiting for customer . A status change can travel on its own. An issue with a new status and no comment still sends, rather than counting as blank and being skipped.

An issue with a comment written on it carries a Ready badge; an issue with only a status change queued and no comment reads Status only . An issue with neither carries no badge at all — nothing has happened to it yet, so there is nothing to announce. An untouched issue is skipped when you send — nothing is posted to it and nothing happens to it. The footer counts everything, so “2 ready · 3 skipped” tells you exactly what is about to go out before you press anything.

h: Copy one comment across the batch
x: Some batches do want the same words everywhere — an incident resolved, a release shipped. Write it in one composer, then copy it across from that composer’s ••• menu. Copy this comment to n issues — fills every other composer in the batch. Clear this comment — empties that one editor. The issue stays in the batch and a queued status change is kept. The number is real , and it excludes the composer you are copying from. If a target already has something in it the entry arms and asks again — Overwrite n comments? — before replacing anything, so a copy can never quietly wipe work you have already done. It is a copy, not a link. Every composer stays independently editable afterwards, so the normal pattern is to paste the shared version everywhere and then change the two that need saying differently. On a service project you get this twice — once for each audience. The menu carries a separate entry for the customer reply and for the internal note, so you can push one set of words to every reply in the batch and a different set to every note. A copy never crosses between them, so a reply can never land in somebody’s internal note — see Copying with two audiences . Updating every issue after an incident or a release? See incident and release updates in Jira .

Clear all comments & status changes sits above the composers and wipes the work rather than the selection : every comment you have written and every status change you have queued. It asks first — the button changes to name exactly what it is about to take — so a stray press costs nothing. It only appears when there is something to clear. Clearing does not send you back to Select — the issues stay picked, so it is the fast way to rewrite a batch. Nothing has been posted at this point, so there is nothing to undo. On a service project there are two more buttons here, for opening and removing internal notes across the batch — see Internal notes across the batch . Attachments work the same way here as anywhere else in the editor — see The comment editor for how files are attached, sized and uploaded.
Send them all in one pass. Everything posts in one pass, and every issue reports back on its own.

Every issue reports its own outcome rather than sharing one tick with the batch. These are all the values a row can take: The row reads What it means Queued… then Posting… In flight. The counters above move with it. Updated The comment posted. Status changed The issue carried a status change and no comment, and it moved. No change needed The move you queued turned out to land on the status the issue was already in, so it was skipped. Nothing was written to the history and no automation was triggered — but it is reported rather than hidden, because you did ask for it. Failed Jira refused, and the row carries the reason Jira gave rather than a generic message. Not sent — out of time The send ran out of time before this issue was started. Nothing was posted to it. The counters above the rows — Updated , Sending , Failed , and Status failed or Not sent when there are any — are running totals of the same values, and update live as the send goes.

Some sends are worth a second look, so the send guard stops and describes the one you are about to make. Every line is counted from your actual batch, and lines with nothing to say do not appear. Two of the limits are refusals rather than warnings. A single file over 150 MB is rejected the moment you attach it, and a send that would write more than 2 GB into Jira is stopped here, before anything posts. Everything else the guard raises is a confirmation you can accept — see Limits for every ceiling in one table. The send guard appears when any one of these is true: the send reaches 10 or more issues any comment in it @mentions someone — they are notified once per issue, so a mention across 25 issues is 25 notifications the attachments come to 50 MB or more , which catches the send that is small in issue count and heavy in bytes any comment is a reply to a customer — at any size, because that one cannot be taken back What it tells you. The heading names the riskiest thing about the send: Email 3 customers? when any reply is customer-facing, Post to 12 issues? when none is, or Move 4 issues? when the batch is status changes only. Underneath, in order: The customers, first and in the warning colour — “3 replies are set to Reply to customer — those customers get them by email. This cannot be undone.” First because it is the only irreversible part: a comment can be deleted, the email has left. What posts, and under whose name — “14 comments post under your name across 9 issues. The other 11 are internal.” Comments and issues are different numbers once a request carries both halves. Watchers — everyone watching each issue is notified. Mentions — called out separately, because a mention notifies once per issue . The storage arithmetic, on a heavy send only — “Keep this tab open. This send adds 1350 MB to Jira (150 MB × 9 issues). Make sure you have room for 1350 MB.” In practice this is the 50 MB line: a comment carrying 50 MB or more of files gets it, whatever the issue count. A second rule catches small files spread far enough to write 250 MB or more into Jira . Confirming acknowledges both halves — that the comment carries files this large, and that your site has room for the multiplied total. Either threshold alone is enough, since a file uploads once however many issues it lands on but its storage multiplies. The × shows only when the issues carry the same files. Video — a note that Jira may take a minute to process it, so a grey placeholder does not read as a failure. What is being skipped — “3 issues with no comment — skipped.” The button repeats the number rather than saying “Confirm”: Post 14 — email 3 customers . Cancel takes focus, Esc closes, and tabbing stays inside — so the dangerous button is never the one your hands land on. A send over 2 GB is refused rather than confirmed. The dialog changes to This send is too large , names your total against the limit, and offers only Back to comments . Nothing is posted — the send stops before it starts rather than failing halfway and leaving some issues done and some not.

You land here as soon as the upload starts, not when posting finishes — on a send carrying files the upload is most of the wait. It reads Step 1 of 2 · Uploading 3 of 8 · 42 MB of 110 MB · 4.1 MB/s · ~0:16 left… , then Step 2 of 2 · Adding to issues , with Cancel under it throughout. Cancelling rolls back. Files already written to issues are removed again, so you are never left with attachments scattered across a dozen issues and no comment explaining them. The same rollback runs if part of the upload fails. When the run finishes the heading names what the send actually did: Comments posted , or Status changes applied when the batch only moved issues, or Issues updated when it was a mix — and it tells you how long it took, down to took 3m 05s . Alongside those, a service-project row carries the audience it reached, and a row whose issue also moved carries the move itself — named at both ends, WAITING FOR SUPPORT → ESCALATED , because afterwards the issue only shows where it ended up, so where it came from is precisely the part you can no longer look up. Retry names what is left — Retry n failed , Send the remaining n , or Retry n unsent when there is some of each. It re-runs only issues where nothing was posted, which is why it skips an issue whose comment landed and whose status change was refused. Done clears the batch. Every row says who saw it. On a service project a row carries SENT TO CUSTOMER , and adds + INTERNAL when that request also carried a note — same colours as everywhere else. That badge is read back off the comment Jira created , not off what was requested — so the screen can tell you when the two disagree. A row can read visibility differs , or + Visibility unknown where Jira did not report on a second comment. Rare, and shown rather than smoothed over. Every row opens its issue: click the issue key or the ↗ on the right and it opens in a new tab — scroll to the bottom of the issue to see the comment or the change that landed. Video takes a while to appear, and that is Jira. Each issue’s copy is processed separately — roughly five to ten minutes for a 100 MB file — and shows a grey box until it finishes. The files are already uploaded; nothing needs re-sending. There is no undo. By the time you could press it a customer’s email has already gone. The send guard replaces it — see the send guard . To remove a comment after the fact, delete it on the issue in Jira. Deleting a customer-facing reply does not unsend the email.
Most sends finish with nothing in the Failed column. When part of one does not land, it is one of three things.

h: When something does not land › The comment posted but the status change was refused
x: A comment that posted and a transition Jira rejected are two different things, counted separately: n status changes failed — the comments posted, change the status in Jira . The column is separate on purpose, because Retry never re-runs an issue whose comment already landed — that would post it twice. Make those moves in Jira instead. The commonest cause is the issue moving in Jira after you picked it, so the transition no longer exists from where it now sits. The row says exactly that.

h: When something does not land › The send ran out of time, or was interrupted
x: A send has a budget. Past it the app stops starting new issues and answers with what it has, marking the rest Not sent — the send ran out of time. Nothing was posted to this issue. Retry covers those alongside anything that failed — a known partial result is safe to retry, which is what the budget buys. If the connection drops and no result comes back at all, Send is held: “the send was interrupted, so we don’t know which comments went through — check the issues in Jira before sending again” , until you press I’ve checked — let me send . Most sends finish with nothing in the Failed column. When something does fail it is usually a permission change, or an issue that was moved or deleted while the batch was running — and the row carries the reason Jira returned. If a retry keeps failing, tell us — send the issue keys and the reason shown against each failed row.

h: The app acts as you, never as itself
x: Every read and every page it creates is made with your Confluence account. The app has no elevated identity and no service account — if Confluence would refuse you, it refuses the app. That is why there is nothing to configure: your existing permissions already describe exactly what the app can do. The practical consequence is that two people running the same clone can get different results, because they can see different spaces.

Two permissions matter, and they can be in different spaces — cloning a template out of one space into another is the normal case. Where What you need Without it The source space Permission to view the space and its pages The page never appears in the Step 1 search, so it cannot be picked as a source. The destination space Permission to add pages The space is rejected when the copies are created. If a space is unreachable the app says so plainly rather than failing silently: Space ‘KEY’ not found or not accessible. Make sure you have permission to view this space. The Step 1 page search is instance-wide , not scoped to the space you are in — but it only ever lists pages you already have permission to read, so the search cannot reveal a page you could not otherwise open.

Copies are ordinary Confluence pages, so Confluence treats them as ordinary pages. If the source page @mentions someone, every copy notifies them again — twenty-five copies means twenty-five notifications per mentioned person, arriving on a short delay. There is no flag to suppress this, so the app warns you on Step 2 before anything is created rather than letting you find out afterwards.

Bulk Page Cloner is an Atlassian Forge app. It installs site-wide and needs a Confluence site administrator, because Forge apps cannot be installed per space. Once installed it is available to everyone, and what each person can actually clone is decided by their own space permissions. It requests six scopes, and nothing else: read:page:confluence — to search and read the page being cloned write:page:confluence — to create the copies read:space:confluence — to list the spaces you can choose from read:label:confluence — to carry the source page’s labels onto each copy write:confluence-content — to attach the copied content storage:app — to hold your selection between steps The app runs entirely on Atlassian infrastructure, so no data leaves your Confluence site and there is no external server to allow-list. Rewrites every field as a numbered series — “Vacation Policy 1”, “Vacation Policy 2”, and so on. h: Naming shortcuts › Copy first to all
x: Fills every field with whatever is in the first one, unchanged and unnumbered. It does nothing at all if the first field is still empty — no error, no partial fill. Because the result is twenty-five identical titles, this one almost always wants Auto-number after it, or a pass through the fields to make them distinct. Confluence will not leave matching titles alone.

Empties every title field in one click. It leaves the copy count alone — you keep the twenty-five empty fields, rather than dropping back to one — so it is the quick way to start the naming over without rebuilding the batch.

Confluence requires page titles to be unique within a space. If two of your titles match, the app says so before you continue — “Some titles match. Confluence auto-numbers duplicate page titles in a space.” — and Auto-number is the one-click fix. If you go ahead anyway nothing breaks: the app renames them on the way out, appending (1) , (2) and so on, which is the same thing Confluence would do to you. Heads-up before you create: the app warns you when a source page @mentions people (each copy notifies them again), for large batches of 10+ pages, and for matching titles before Confluence auto-numbers them.

Put a parent’s child pages in order in one step, and move many pages at once. Confluence adds each new page to the end of its parent’s list, and its page tree moves one page per drag. Putting a long list in order means dragging every page by hand. Page Order sorts the child pages of any page, folder or space in one step: A to Z, Z to A, newest, oldest or recently updated, with numbers in titles sorted as numbers. Drag across pages to select a group, then drag it to a new spot, drop it into another page, or send it to another parent or space with Move to… . Child pages always go with their parent. Nothing changes in Confluence until you press Save changes . h: The app acts as you, never as itself
x: Every read, move and rename is made with your Confluence account: in the browser while you arrange pages, and in the app’s backend while a save runs, acting for the person whose tab started it. The app has no service account, no elevated identity and no way to act for someone who is not using it — if Confluence would refuse you, it refuses the app. That is why there is nothing to configure. Your existing Confluence permissions already describe exactly what the app can do, and it never does more than you could do by hand. Two people opening the same parent can see different pages and be allowed different things.

Seeing a space’s page tree and changing it need different permissions. To What you need Without it See a space and its pages Permission to view the space The space is not listed under Choose a space to organize or in Move to… , and its pages never appear. Change the order, or move pages out of a space Space admin , or Manage all content on sites that use space roles — what Confluence’s own Move needs You see the order but can’t select, drag, sort or save, and a banner says why. Move pages into another space Whatever Confluence asks of you there, checked as each page moves Those moves are refused at save and named in the result. Everything else in the save still goes ahead. The banner reads You can see this order but not change it. Moving pages needs Space admin or Manage all content in Team Handbook. Confluence has no single “move” permission an app can ask about, so the app checks for those two space permissions when the organizer opens — the pair Confluence’s own Move relies on.

Page restrictions apply exactly as they do everywhere else in Confluence. A page you can’t view never appears — not in the list, not in the page tree, not in Move to… . The app can’t select it, sort it or reveal its title. A page you can view but Confluence won’t let you move is tried at save, refused, and left where it is. The pages around it still move, and the result names it: 6 pages moved. 2 pages couldn’t be moved: “Travel”, “Security”. They may be restricted, or you may not have permission. One refused page never stops the rest of a save. Each page is moved on its own, so a save does everything you are allowed to do and lists what it couldn’t.

Some refusals come from Confluence itself and apply to everyone, site admins included. The app checks for them before a move is staged, so nobody finds out only when saving. More than 1,000 items beneath a page. Confluence won’t move a page like that at all, not even with its own Move, so it can’t go into another page or space. The app marks it Too big to move out . It can still be dragged up or down among its siblings: the pages around it move instead. Two pages like that can’t swap places, so they keep their current order and everything else is arranged around them. Titles are unique within a space, ignoring case. Moving a page into a space that already has its title is refused, so the app asks first: Rename and move , to a free title such as “Travel (1)” like the one Confluence’s own Move suggests, or Leave it out . A page can’t go inside one of its own child pages. That move is left out, and the panel beside the list says why. Every limit, and what happens at each, is on the Limits page.

Page Order is an Atlassian Forge app. It installs site-wide and needs a Confluence site administrator, because Forge apps cannot be installed per space. Once installed it is available to everyone, and what each person can change is decided by their own space permissions, above. There is no settings screen and no admin page. It requests seven scopes, and nothing else: write:confluence-content — to move pages, with Confluence’s move API write:page:confluence — to rename a page whose title is already used in the space it is moving to read:hierarchical-content:confluence — to read a parent’s child pages in page tree order read:page:confluence — to read pages’ titles, parents and dates read:folder:confluence — to read folders’ titles, parents and dates read:space:confluence — to list spaces, and check whether you can move pages in one search:confluence — to find a page by title in Move to… , count what is beneath a page, and show when each space was last updated It has no app storage, no database, no triggers and no background jobs, and it sends nothing outside Atlassian — it carries the Runs on Atlassian badge, so there is no external server to allow-list. A save runs only while the tab that started it stays open. Uninstalling from Apps → Manage apps leaves nothing behind, because nothing was stored; pages stay where the last save put them. The step-by-step install is under Get started → Installation .

Page Order is free for teams of 10 users or fewer , and billed per user through the Atlassian Marketplace above that, on your existing Atlassian invoice. Billing is Atlassian’s — the app never sees a payment detail, and there is nothing to set up inside it. The licence is checked every time the app opens. If the site’s subscription is not active — a trial that ended, or a subscription that lapsed — every way in shows Page Order needs an active subscription on this site. Ask your Confluence admin to start a trial or subscribe from Manage apps. and nothing can be sorted or moved. Pages already saved are unaffected: their order is Confluence’s own.

h: Setting it up › Is there anything to configure after installing?
x: No. The app has no settings screen and adds no admin page to Confluence. What each person can do with it is decided entirely by the Confluence permissions they already have — see the Admin guide .

h: Setting it up › Who can use it once it is installed?
x: Everyone on the site can open it and see the pages they could already see. Changing the order in a space needs Space admin , or Manage all content on sites that use space roles — the same as Confluence’s own Move. Without either, the app shows the order but won’t let you change it.

h: Setting it up › Can I restrict it to certain spaces?
x: Not from inside the app, because there is nothing to configure. Confluence’s own permissions are the control: someone without Space admin or Manage all content in a space can’t change anything there with the app either.

h: Setting it up › Will it slow my Confluence site down?
x: It runs on Atlassian’s own infrastructure and only does anything while someone has it open. It adds no background jobs and no triggers — just three entries: Organize Child Pages in the page menu, Page Order in each space’s sidebar, and Page Order for Confluence under Apps.

h: Setting it up › Does it work on Confluence Server or Data Center?
x: No. It is built on Atlassian Forge, which is Cloud only.

h: Setting it up › Where do I open it from?
x: Three places: Organize Child Pages in any page’s ••• menu, Page Order in a space’s sidebar, or Page Order for Confluence under Apps — see Where to open it .

h: Sorting and moving › Which sorts are there?
x: Five: A to Z and Z to A by title, Newest first and Oldest first by date created, and Recently updated first by last update. Sort numbers by value is on to start with, so titles sort 2, 9, 10 rather than 10, 2, 9; untick it to sort by letters only.

h: Sorting and moving › Can I sort only some of the pages?
x: Yes. Select two or more pages and Sort all becomes Sort N selected . Only those pages are sorted, in the places they already held; every other page stays where it is.

h: Sorting and moving › Can I sort every level below a page?
x: Yes. In the Sort all menu, tick Include every level below . When you save, every parent beneath is sorted the same way, up to 500 parents per sort. Past that the result says where to carry on: Stopped after 500 parents; open a page further down and sort from there for the rest.

h: Sorting and moving › Do child pages move with their parent?
x: Yes, always, as they do in Confluence. Dragging a page into another page, dropping it on the page tree or using Move to… takes everything beneath it along. Reordering pages under the same parent doesn’t change what is beneath any of them.

h: Sorting and moving › Can I move pages to another space?
x: Yes, with Move to… : choose any space you can see, then the page to put them under (or the top level of that space), and whether they go First or Last . If a title is already used in that space, the app asks first: Rename and move , to a free title such as “Travel (1)” like the one Confluence’s own Move suggests, or Leave it out .

h: Sorting and moving › What about folders, whiteboards and databases?
x: They share the page tree with pages, so they appear in the list and can be reordered and moved like pages. Pages and folders can also take other pages into them. Date sorts put whiteboards, databases and Smart links last, because the app doesn’t read their dates.

h: Sorting and moving › How many pages can I move at once?
x: Up to 1,000 page moves per save, every one listed before you save. Include every level below is limited by parents instead (up to 500), because its moves are worked out while saving. The list itself isn’t capped: a parent with thousands of child pages loads in full. A rearrangement that needs more than 1,000 moves saves the first 1,000 and tells you to Sort again and save to finish . More than 1,000 pages moving to new parents can’t be saved until you cancel some with × and move them in a second save. See Limits .

h: Sorting and moving › Why does a page say “Too big to move out”?
x: It has more than 1,000 items beneath it, and Confluence can’t move a page like that at all — not even with its own Move — so it can’t go into another page or space. You can still drag it up or down among its siblings; the pages around it move instead. Two pages like that can’t swap places, so they keep their current order and everything else is arranged around them. To move one out, move some of its child pages out first.

h: Sorting and moving › Can I change several parents in one save?
x: Yes. Changes stay staged while you open other parents, and Save changes saves them all, up to 100 parents in one save. Past that, the app asks you to save some of the changes first, then the rest.

h: Saving › When does anything change in Confluence?
x: Only when you press Save changes . Sorting, dragging and Move to… stage changes in the Unsaved changes panel. Discard drops them all, and × on a move cancels just that one.

h: Saving › Can I undo a save?
x: No — and Confluence can’t undo a move either. That is why the panel shows exactly what a save will do first: each change opens to list its pages, and a parent whose order changes shows each page’s old and new position. To put pages back, sort or move them again and save.

h: Saving › What if I close the tab while it’s saving?
x: The save stops there. A save runs only while its tab is open, and the panel says so while it works: Moving a lot of pages can take a few minutes. Keep this tab open until it’s done; closing it stops the save. Pages already moved stay moved. Open the organizer again and the list shows the order as it is now; sort or move again and save, and only what is still out of place moves.

h: Saving › How long does a save take?
x: Each page is moved with its own call to Confluence, so the time grows with the number of moves: a short list saves in seconds, and hundreds of moves take a few minutes. The panel counts the moves as they go.

h: Saving › What if someone else changes the pages while I’m working?
x: Before saving, the app reads again every parent you opened that the save will change. If any of them changed since you opened it, nothing is saved: These pages changed since you opened them, so nothing was saved. Load the latest order drops your unsaved changes and shows the order as it is now, so you can make them again on top of it.

h: Saving › What if some pages can’t be moved?
x: The rest still save. Each page is moved on its own, so one refusal never stops the others, and the result names the pages that didn’t move and says why — usually a page restriction, a missing permission, or more than 1,000 items beneath the page.

h: Saving › Does moving a page change its last-updated date?
x: No. A move doesn’t make a new version of the page, so Recently updated first still reflects real edits. Renaming a page to clear a title clash does make a new version, like any rename.

h: Confluence’s own limits › Rate limits and a busy Confluence
x: Confluence answers with a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) when the app is over Atlassian’s rate limit, which is one budget shared by every site using the app, and now and then with a server error. Instead of failing on one busy moment, the app waits as long as Confluence asks, or backs off, and tries again: Reads are retried up to five times on a rate limit, and twice on a server error. Moves are retried up to five times on a rate limit, and once on a server error. During a save , each wait is kept to 3 seconds so a stretch stays inside Forge’s time limit. A page still rate-limited after its retries is reported as not moved, and the save carries on with the rest. A stretch that fails outright is tried twice more, 2 and then 4 seconds later; if it still fails, the save stops and shows the error. Three stretches in a row that make no progress stop it too: “Confluence is responding too slowly, so the save stopped.” Either way, pages already moved stay moved. A read that is still rate-limited after its retries says “Confluence is busy. Wait a minute and try again.”

Page Order is an Atlassian Forge app for Confluence Cloud. It has two parts, and both run on Atlassian’s own infrastructure: The organizer you work in. This is the screen Confluence shows when you open Organize Child Pages from a page’s ••• menu, Page Order in a space’s sidebar, or Page Order for Confluence under Apps (see Where to open it ). It reads the page tree for you to browse and holds your changes until you save. One function on Forge. This is the part that moves the pages when you press Save changes . Each move goes from there straight to Confluence, instead of making a round trip through your browser. The app declares no external domains, so it has no way to send anything outside Atlassian: it is a Runs on Atlassian app. Even its icon is bundled with the app instead of being fetched from somewhere else. It follows your Confluence theme, light or dark.

Every call Page Order makes to Confluence is made as the person signed in: in the browser through Forge’s requestConfluence , and during a save through api.asUser() . It never acts as the app itself, and never for someone who isn’t at the screen — there is no impersonation. So Confluence applies your own permissions, exactly as if you had moved the pages by hand: You see only what you can see. Pages you can’t view don’t appear in the list, the page tree or Move to… . Moving needs Confluence’s own permission. Confluence lets you move pages in a space if you are a space admin there, or have Manage all content where space roles are on. A move Confluence turns down, such as a restricted page or a space where you can’t move pages, fails on its own and is named in the result. The rest of the save goes ahead. The Admin guide covers these permissions in detail.

x: Before a move to another parent is added to Unsaved changes , the app checks for what Confluence would refuse: a page with more than 1,000 items beneath it, a title already used in the other space, and a destination inside one of the pages being moved. h: How a save works › The steps of a save
x: Check the order first. The app reads the current order of every parent your changes touch and compares it with the order you were shown when you made your changes. If anything changed since then, someone else moving a page for example, nothing is saved and a banner says “These pages changed since you opened them, so nothing was saved.” Load the latest order starts you again from what Confluence has now. Move pages to their new parents. Pages you chose to rename, because their title is already used in the space they are going to, are renamed first. Then each page moves, lining up after the one before it so the group lands together, at the top or the bottom as you chose. Their child pages move with them. Apply each parent’s new order. The app keeps the longest run of pages already in the right order relative to each other and moves only the rest, so the count in Unsaved changes is the number of pages that really move. Within one parent the moves run one after another, because Confluence loses track of sibling positions when several move at once; up to three different parents are worked on at the same time. Afterwards the app reads the order back from Confluence, and if anything landed out of place (a page couldn’t move, or someone moved one meanwhile), it plans again from what Confluence actually has and puts it right once. Sort every level below. If you sorted with Include every level below , each parent beneath the one you sorted is sorted the same way, working down a level at a time, up to three parents at once.

Release date: October 4, 2026 · Version: 3.3.0 The first release of Page Order for Confluence. Confluence adds new pages to the end of the list and moves pages one drag at a time; Page Order puts a whole list in order in one step, moves many pages at once, and lists every change before anything is saved.

Organize Child Pages — in any page’s ••• menu, opening in a dialog on that page’s child pages. Page Order — in each space’s sidebar, starting at the space’s top level. Page Order for Confluence — under Apps : choose any space to organize, most recently updated first.

Sort all — A to Z, Z to A, Newest first, Oldest first (by date created) or Recently updated first (by last update), for every child page of a parent in one step. Sort numbers by value — 2, 9, 10 rather than 10, 2, 9. Sort n selected — select some pages and only those are sorted, among themselves, in the places they already held. Include every level below — sorts each parent beneath the one you sorted, the same way.

Drag across pages to select them , then drag the group to a new spot; a line shows where it will land. Drop pages on the middle of a page to move them inside it, or onto a page in the page tree beside the list. Marks on every changed row — ▲ and ▼ show how far a page moves, and Moving in marks pages arriving from elsewhere.

Any parent, in any space you can see — choose the space, then the page to put them under, and whether they go First or Last . Child pages move with their parent. Titles that clash are handled the way Confluence’s own Move handles them — when a title is already used in the other space, rename and move (as “Expenses (1)”, say) or leave that page out.

Nothing changes in Confluence until you save — every change waits in Unsaved changes , where each one opens to list its pages, × cancels a move, and Discard clears the lot. Up to 1,000 page moves per save , using as few moves as possible. Each new order is read back from Confluence afterwards and put right if anything landed out of place. Refusals caught before you save — a page with more than 1,000 items beneath it, a title already used in the other space (unless you choose to rename it), or a page that would go inside its own child page is left out, with the reason. Saves run as you, while your tab is open — closing the tab stops the save, and pages already moved stay moved.

Acts only as you — Confluence’s own permissions apply, so people move only the pages they could already move by hand. Stores nothing — no database and no background jobs, and it runs on Atlassian with nothing sent outside it. The only thing remembered is whether the page tree is shown, in your own browser.
